chapters.summary: Types of numbers on the number line: Natural (N), Whole (W), Integers (Z), Rational (Q). Introduces constructing the collections and inclusion relations.

key_definitions.Rational number: r is rational if r = p/q with integers p,q and q ≠ 0 (denoted Q)

chapters.summary: Defines irrational numbers (cannot be expressed as p/q). Examples: √2, √3, √5, π, and constructed non-repeating decimals. Real numbers R = rationals ∪ irrationals.

key_definitions.Irrational number: a number not expressible as p/q (integers p,q, q≠0)
key_definitions.Real number: Every point on number line; union of rational and irrational numbers (denoted R)

chapters.notes: Historical notes: Pythagoreans, Cantor & Dedekind (correspondence between real numbers and points on line).

chapters.chapter: 1.3 Real Numbers and their Decimal Expansions
chapters.summary: Decimal-expansion characterization: rationals ⇄ (terminating OR repeating) decimals; irrationals ⇄ (non-terminating, non-repeating). Shows how division remainders produce repeating blocks and demonstrates methods to express repeating decimals as p/q.

Closure properties: rationals closed under +,-,×,÷(≠0). Irrationals satisfy algebraic laws but sums/products with rationals/irrationals may or may not be irrational; examples and rationalisation of denominators using conjugates.
key_points: irrational ± irrational may be rational or irrational

chapters.summary: Worked examples on decimal expansions, locating √n on number line geometrically (using Pythagoras) and constructing square-root spiral; exercises for classification and conversions.
exercise_types: Find rational numbers between given rationals
Construct square-root spiral and locate roots geometrically

chapters.summary: Concise recap of definitions and main properties: rational vs irrational decimal forms, real numbers, and a few algebraic identities for positive reals.

important_points: Decimal expansion of rational: terminating or repeating
Decimal expansion of irrational: non-terminating non-repeating

formulas: rational: r = p/q, p,q ∈ Z, q ≠ 0
decimal characterization: rational ⇄ (terminating OR repeating); irrational ⇄ non-terminating non-repeating
geometric location of √n via Pythagoras (construction described on pages with Fig.1.6–1.13)
identities for rationalising: (a+b)(a−b) = a^2 − b^2 (used for conjugates)
examples_highlighted: 1/7 = 0.142857... repeating block due to remainder cycle
Construction of √x on number line (geometric method for any x>0)
meta.exercises_sample: Exercise 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4 (classification, decimal expansion conversions, rationalisation problems).

chapters.summary: Definition of polynomial in one variable: p(x)=a_n x^n + ... + a_1 x + a_0 with a_n ≠ 0. Terms, coefficients, monomial/binomial/trinomial, degree of polynomial; linear, quadratic, cubic definitions and canonical forms (ax^2+bx+c, ax^3+bx^2+cx+d).

key_definitions.Polynomial: algebraic expression in x with non-negative integer exponents

chapters.summary: Value p(a) is the value of polynomial at x=a. Zero/root defined as p(c)=0. Properties: linear polynomial has unique zero; non-zero constant has no zero; zero polynomial has every real as zero.
examples: If p(x)=x−1 then p(1)=0 so x=1 is root
Verification examples: p(x)=x^2−2x has zeros 0 and 2

chapters.summary: Remainder theorem and Factor theorem: remainder when p(x) divided by x−a is p(a); x−a is factor iff p(a)=0. Methods to factor quadratics (split middle term) and cubics (find one linear factor by trial then reduce).
key_methods: Splitting the middle term for ax^2+bx+c: find two numbers with product ac and sum b
Use Factor Theorem to test possible rational roots (factors of constant term) then divide
examples: 6x^2+17x+5 = (3x+1)(2x+5) (splitting method and factor theorem both shown)
x^3 − 23x^2 + 142x − 120 factorised by finding x−1 as factor then factoring quadratic

chapters.summary: Cubic identities and symmetric formulas: (x+y)^3, x^3+y^3, x^3+y^3+z^3−3xyz factorisation, expansion of (x+y+z)^2 etc. Exercises include factorising sums of cubes and using identities.

Recap of polynomial definitions, degree, classification, zeroes, factor theorem and key algebraic identities. Exercises test recognition, evaluation at values, zero verification, factorisation and application to dimensions/areas/volumes.
exercise_types: Apply identities to evaluate expressions and find dimensions from algebraic area/volume forms

formulas: Remainder Theorem: remainder on division by (x−a) is p(a)
Factor Theorem: x−a is factor ⇄ p(a)=0
Common identities: (x+y)^2, (x+y)^3, x^3−y^3, x^3+y^3+z^3−3xyz (see chapter summary)
examples_highlighted: Finding degree of polynomials (examples x^5 − x^4 + 3 etc.)
Cubic factorisation via trial roots (list of possible integer factors of the constant term tested)
meta.exercises_sample: Exercise 2.1, 2.2 (classification, value evaluation, zero verification), further exercises on factorisation and identity verification.
